# Vacuum Routing for Sea Foam Treatment on Mazda 3 (1.6L BKL3)

Treating internal engine components with additives like Sea Foam is a common maintenance strategy, particularly when addressing carbon buildup or stale fuel issues. However, the routing method varies significantly between direct injection (DI) and port fuel injection (PFI) architectures. Your 2010 Mazda 3 with the 1.6L BKL3 engine utilizes a Port Fuel Injection system. This distinction is critical because PFI engines have intake valves that are not washed by fuel during combustion, making them susceptible to carbon accumulation over time. Consequently, introducing a solvent like Sea Foam directly into the intake manifold is a valid and often recommended approach for these specific units.

The photograph you provided shows a vacuum line located at the throttle body. In many Mazda 3 models equipped with the BKL3 engine, this line connects the top of the throttle body to the Intake Manifold Runner Control (IMRC) actuator or a dedicated vacuum port on the intake plenum. To administer Sea Foam via this route, you must identify the source of vacuum pressure. On these engines, a robust and consistent vacuum source is typically available at the front of the intake manifold runner control valve or directly from the intake plenum itself.

Connecting the aerosol can to this line requires careful consideration of flow dynamics. The vacuum port acts as a suction point; when the engine creates negative pressure, it draws fluid from your container into the airflow path. If you attempt to use the line shown in your image for liquid transfer, ensure that the connection is sealed tightly. A loose fitting will result in unmetered air entering the intake, which can lean out the fuel mixture and cause rough idling or hesitation. Ideally, you should utilize a dedicated vacuum nipple on the intake manifold if one exists, rather than relying solely on existing lines for high-volume fluid transfer. If using an existing line, ensure the container has a vent mechanism to prevent a vacuum lock that would stop the flow of the additive.

Regarding your plan to split the dosage: placing half the can in the gas tank addresses fuel system cleanliness and injector deposits, while the remaining portion in the intake targets valve carbon. This dual-application method is standard for comprehensive cleaning campaigns. The amount you pour into the crankcase (half a can) is generally sufficient for most 1.6L engines, but monitor the oil level closely after the engine has cooled down to ensure it does not exceed the maximum mark.

There is a specific nuance regarding the "spray" method mentioned in older tutorials. Those guides often suggest spraying directly into the throttle body while the engine is running or off. While effective for quick cleaning, it requires a large quantity of product and carries a risk of flooding the intake if not done precisely. Since you noted that spray cans are unavailable in your region and only motor treatment (liquid concentrates) are accessible, using the vacuum line method is actually the superior choice here. It ensures a controlled, metered dose of the liquid additive directly into the intake tract without the mess or volume requirements of aerosol spraying.

Finally, verify that this routing applies to your specific trim level. While the 2.0L and 2.3L engines share similar architecture, the 1.6L BKL3 is distinct. The vacuum line you identified is consistent with PFI setups for this generation, but always double-check against a service manual or a verified forum thread for the BKL3 specifically to confirm there are no model-year specific changes to the IMRC actuator location. If the line you have access to leads directly to the runner control valve, it provides a reliable path to the intake runners where the fuel-air mixture is formed.
